fetched_contents.text: Investigating urban–rural disparities in tuberculosis treatment outcome in England and Wales SUMMARY The purpose of this study was to compare the occurrence of tuberculosis (TB) and the outcome of treatment between TB patients living in urban and rural areas. Cases of TB reported from 2001 to 2003 in England and Wales were assigned to a rural or urban area classification. The outcome of interest, non-completion of treatment, was investigated to determine the odds ratio for urban vs. rural residence. The effects of age, sex, ethnicity, place of birth, time since arrival in the United Kingdom, disease site, isoniazid resistance and previous diagnosis were adjusted for by multivariable logistic regression. Crude odds ratios showed a significantly higher level of treatment non-completion in rural areas. These results became non-significant (OR 1·02, 95% CI 0·83–1·26, P=0·82) after adjusting for the confounding effects of ethnic group and age. In England and Wales residence in a rural location is not an independent determinant of TB treatment outcome failure. INTRODUCTION The burden of disease in urban populations is generally considered to be greater than in rural populations. The evidence on quality of care, however, suggests that service accessibility is poorer in rural areas [1, 2]. While health services in urban settings may be within relatively easy reach, patients in rural areas often have to travel long distances. It is not known whether levels of access to tuberculosis (TB) services differ between urban and rural areas in the United Kingdom. There are reasons why the outcome of care may be worse in urban or rural areas. Variation in the occurrence of TB between urban and rural areas has been reported from various countries [3, 4]. In the United Kingdom, TB is more common in urban areas [5]. The higher case load in urban areas may result in services based in cities generally having greater clinical experience in the management of TB when compared with rural services which may affect the overall quality of care available to patients in rural settings. In contrast, many TB patients in urban settings are from highly deprived communities. Social disadvantage in urban areas may contribute to a poorer outcome. This study was undertaken to determine whether a difference exists in treatment completion rates between urban and rural areas and to investigate the factors associated with any variation in outcome. MATERIAL AND METHODS Study subjects, definitions and data sources All patients reported to the national enhanced TB surveillance system from 2001 to 2003 in England and Wales were eligible for inclusion. TB cases include all patients whose diagnosis was confirmed by bacteriological culture or those who have clinical/radiological/histopathological features suggestive of TB and the clinician had taken the decision to treat the patient with a full course of anti-TB therapy. Outcome data were collected 12 months after the date of notification or start of treatment. Outcome was categorized as either treatment completed or treatment not completed. The ‘treatment not completed’ category includes patients whose reported outcome was death, lost to follow-up, transferred out, still on treatment, treatment stopped or ‘unknown’. The residential postcodes of all cases with an outcome reported were geo-coded. Cases were assigned to a rural or urban area based on the Rural and Urban Classification 2004 Office of National Statistics (ONS) (see Fig.). Data from the 2001 census were used to derive population denominator estimates for urban and rural areas. Patients with multidrug-resistant disease were excluded from the analysis because current treatment regimens recommend a course of therapy of at least 18 months for any patient with rifampicin resistance. Information on the treatment outcome of patients at 18 or 24 months is currently not collected by the national TB surveillance system. Analysis The relative risk of TB in urban compared to rural areas was determined. The outcome of interest, non-completion of treatment within 12 months of starting treatment or notification, was investigated by logistic regression to determine odds ratios for urban vs. rural residence. A multivariable model was fitted controlling for the effect of all factors significant in the univariable analysis. Bivariable analysis was used to sequentially examine the confounding effect of age, sex, ethnic group, place of birth/time since arrival in the United Kingdom, disease site, drug resistance and previous diagnosis. RESULTS A total of 19 836 cases were reported. Of these an outcome was reported on 16 784 (85%) patients. A residential postcode was available for 16 109 cases (96%) and they were mapped to a rural or an urban area. The median age of the population was 36 years (interquartile range 26–55 years). The majority of cases lived in urban areas (96·7%), were male (54·9%), of Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi (36·8%), or black African (21·5%) ethnicity and born outside the United Kingdom (68·5%). fetched_contents.text: A systematic synthesis of direct costs to treat and manage tuberculosis disease applied to California, 2015 Abstract Background The cost of treating and managing cases of active tuberculosis (TB) disease—from diagnosis to treatment completion—is needed by agencies working on public health budgets, resource allocation and cost-effectiveness analysis. Although components of TB costs have been published in the United States (US), no recent study has assessed overall costs for TB care and potential gaps. To systematically review the US literature for costs of treating and managing cases of active TB disease, adjust these costs to current (2015) values, and assess gaps. We quantified total direct costs—from the perspective of the health care payer—of the treatment and case management of active TB disease. Estimates were based on published figures in the US, and operational data of the California Department of Public Health. Result The average direct cost of treating and managing a TB case was $34,600 in 2015. The average cost of a multidrug-resistant TB case was $110,900. Health care spending for treating and case managing TB patients in California amounted to approximately $75.6 million for the 2133 new cases reported in 2015. Most published cost estimates were based on data from the 1990s. Conclusion TB is resource-intensive to treat and manage. Our synthesis provides inputs for budgets and economic analyses. New studies to provide original cost data are needed to better reflect current clinical and public health practices. Electronic supplementary material The online version of this article (doi:10.1186/s13104-017-2754-y) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users. Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a substantial public health challenge in the United States (US), with 9563 new cases of the disease reported in 2015 [1]. The costs of treating and managing tuberculosis are key inputs for economic evaluations to assess the cost-effectiveness of public health interventions. Health policy-making, public health department budget planning, and advocacy efforts also benefit from accurate estimates of TB costs, but recently published information on their magnitude in the US setting is limited. We reviewed the literature for original US-based data on the direct health care costs of treating and managing TB disease, and adjusted costs to 2015 US dollars. Our main objective was to generate comprehensive, literature-based, inflation-adjusted medical cost estimates. A secondary objective was to qualitatively assess gaps in the current knowledge of TB costs, to guide future research on the topic. Methods We performed a literature review, identified and adjusted the average costs of TB reported in the literature, and described gaps and trends in reported costs. We used an ingredients framework, in which the total cost of a program or intervention is estimated by summing each component of cost [2]. The six direct cost components in our analysis were (1) hospitalization, (2) inpatient physician services, (3) outpatient physician services, (4) outpatient case management (clinic visits and case management personnel time for directly observed therapy), (5) laboratory and imaging tests, and (6) anti-TB medications. First, we reviewed the literature for published original cost estimates for any of these components. We filled gaps in the literature (i.e., a component for which we found no published cost) by using federal Medicare data to calculate estimates based on service utilization characteristics of an average case, according to TB surveillance and operational data in California. We adjusted all estimates for inflation to reflect prices in 2015 using specific components of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as detailed in the online appendix (Additional file 1). Finally, we stratified our analysis by multidrug-resistant TB (MDR TB resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin) and drug-susceptible TB because MDR TB is substantially more costly than drug-susceptible TB. We searched the Scopus electronic database in January 2016 for articles published between 1990 and 2015 that reported original data on direct costs of tuberculosis treatment and case management. We used the search term “tuberculosis cost” and limited results to articles in the life sciences, health sciences, and social sciences and humanities. We limited the search to English-language articles, and US-based costs. We chose the narrow focus of US-based costs because the health care system in the US is different than that in other low TB incidence/high income countries (e.g. Western European nations). Second, two authors (PO, LP) reviewed the titles and abstracts of the articles and excluded those in which the term cost was used in terms other than financial cost (e.g., fitness costs to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis organism due to genetic mutations), and TB disease in animals. The same authors reviewed the remaining articles in full to identify those with original estimates of direct costs of any TB cost component (as opposed to secondary cost estimates citing other work). The perspective of our analysis was the health care payer of medical services. We limited our estimates to the costs of treatment and case management of active TB cases, and did not include any of the following: indirect and societal costs (e.g., productivity losses incurred by TB patients); costs of the workup leading to diagnosis of TB; or costs of contact investigation. We also excluded estimates related to inpatient care that were based on charge data, because hospital charges are considered unreliable proxies for costs. If an article reported the cost of an episode of a component, we adjusted this cost to a per-patient basis by multiplying it by the average utilization, based on surveillance data in the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) TB registry [3], and CDPH operational databases. fetched_contents.text: Cost of TB services in the public and private sectors in Georgia Show available content in Abstract BACKGROUND: Patient-centred care along with optimal financing of inpatient and outpatient services are the main priorities of the Georgia National TB Programme (NTP). This paper presents TB diagnostics and treatment unit cost, their comparison with NTP tariffs and how the study findings informed TB financing policy. METHODS: Top-down (TD) and bottom-up (BU) mean unit costs for TB interventions by episode of care were calculated. TD costs were compared with NTP tariffs, and variations in these and the unit costs cost composition between public and private facilities was assessed. RESULTS: Outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs. Unit costs in private facilities were higher compared with public providers. There was very little difference between per-day costs for drug-susceptible treatment and NTP tariffs in case of inpatient services. Treatment day financing exceeded actual costs in the capital (public facility) for drug-resistant TB, and this was lower in the regions. CONCLUSION: Use of reliable unit costs for TB services at policy discussions led to a shift from per-day payment to a diagnosis-related group model in TB inpatient financing in 2020. A next step will be informing policy decisions on outpatient TB care financing to reduce the existing gap between funding and costs. Keywords: tuberculosis, unit costs, top-down approach, financing, Georgia ---------------------------------------- Prior to 2016, Georgia was among one of the high burden countries for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB), but has since achieved significant progress in its TB response.1 The incidence rate for all forms of TB dropped from 99 to 74 per 100,000 population (range 62–67) during 2015–2019.2,3 With 2,169 notified TB cases in a population of 3.7 million people in 2019, TB drug resistance remains a key challenge for the National TB Programme (NTP). The proportion of rifampicin-resistant/multidrugresistant TB (RR/MDR-TB) remains at 12% (range 10–14) among new cases, but dropped from 39% to 32% (range 28–37) among previously treated cases since 2015.2,3 TB services are delivered by a mix of public and private service providers. Specialised TB public facilities are concentrated in Tbilisi City and a couple of other urban areas, while in the districts and regional centres there is a network of stand-alone private facilities where TB services are integrated into general health care. The traditional financing approach of fixed tariffs per bed-day for drug-susceptible (DS-) or drug-resistant (DR-) TB inpatient care has created a perverse incentive for hospitalisation for diagnosis and DS-TB treatment, and prolonged hospital stays. Although this trend has decreased over the last decade,4,5 25% of DS-TB and 80% of DR-TB patients were hospitalised for respectively 30 and 60 days in 2017–2018.3 Guided by the National TB Strategy for 2019–2020, and in line with the WHO Global END TB Strategy,6 Georgia is moving towards a patient-centred approach by reducing hospitalisations and shifting to the outpatient care model.7 Outpatient care is financed through case-based payment for TB diagnostics and contact screening, and monthly DS- or DR-TB vouchers for institutions per patient treated. Improving the efficiency of TB financing has become especially important during the transition away from Global Fund support. To address inefficiencies, the Ministry of Internally Displaced persons from the Occupied Territories, Labour, Health and Social Affairs (MoILHSA) and the National Center for Disease Control and Public Health (NCDC) commissioned a project to develop policy recommendations on optimal financing of TB hospital care by 2020. Implementation of the policies around patient-centred care and optimal financing of inpatient and outpatient care require accurate and current unit cost estimates for TB services,7 which were lacking in Georgia. Value TB, a Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (Seattle, WA, USA) funded multi-country study to estimate the unit costs of TB services from the health service providers’ perspective, was conducted in Georgia in 2019. This paper presents unit cost estimates derived from that study, compares Value TB unit costs with the budgeted NTP values (tariffs) for diagnostics and treatment, and illustrates how Value TB findings informed policy discussions around optimising investments in TB care. The paper also presents cost variations and cost drivers for further policy discussions. fetched_contents.text: Financial burden for tuberculosis patients in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review Abstract In order to inform the development of appropriate strategies to improve financial risk protection, we conducted a systematic literature review of the financial burden of tuberculosis (TB) faced by patients and affected families. The mean total costs ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847. On average, 20% (range 0–62%) of the total cost was due to direct medical costs, 20% (0–84%) to direct non-medical costs, and 60% (16–94%) to income loss. Half of the total cost was incurred before TB treatment. On average, the total cost was equivalent to 58% (range 5–306%) of reported annual individual and 39% (4–148%) of reported household income. Cost as percentage of income was particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB. Commonly reported coping mechanisms included taking a loan and selling household items. The total cost of TB for patients can be catastrophic. Income loss often constitutes the largest financial risk for patients. Apart from ensuring that healthcare services are fairly financed and delivered in a way that minimises direct and indirect costs, there is a need to ensure that TB patients and affected families receive appropriate income replacement and other social protection interventions. Short abstract Costs and income loss put people with TB at financial risk, requiring mitigation with social protection interventions http://ow.ly/sqgRU Introduction An estimated 100 million people fall below the poverty line each year because of the financial burden of disease [1]. Tuberculosis (TB), which mostly affects the poorest of the poor, is an example of a disease that can substantially contribute to the disease poverty trap [2, 3]. Most countries aim to provide TB diagnosis and treatment free of charge within public health services. Access to free TB care has expanded substantially over the past two decades through national efforts and global financial support [4]. However, many TB patients and families are still facing very high direct and indirect costs due to TB illness and care-seeking, hampering access and putting people at risk of financial ruin or further impoverishment [5, 6]. The World Health Organization (WHO) is developing a post-2015 Global TB Strategy, which highlights the need for all countries to progress towards universal health coverage to ensure “universal access to needed health services without financial hardship in paying for them,” [7] as well as social protection mechanisms for “income replacement and social support in the event of illness” [8, 9]. One of the tentative global targets for the strategy is “no TB-affected family facing catastrophic costs due to TB”, to be reached globally by 2020 [10]. This target reflects the anticipated combined financial risk protection effect of the progressive realisation of both universal health coverage and social protection. Universal health coverage has long been on the global TB control agenda, which stresses the need for universally accessible, affordable and patient-centred services [2, 11–13]. Social protection has emerged more recently as a key policy area for TB care and prevention [10, 14–17]. Social protection involves schemes to cover costs beyond direct medical costs, including compensation of lost income. Examples of social protection schemes include sickness insurance, disability grants, other conditional or unconditional cash transfers, food assistance, travel vouchers and other support packages [14]. Such schemes exist in most countries, but may not be fully implemented due to inadequate financing or insufficient capacities of the healthcare and social welfare systems [18]. Furthermore, they may not include TB patients among those eligible [10, 14, 17]. In order to inform the development of appropriate strategies for improved access and financial risk protection for people with TB, we have undertaken a systematic literature review on medical costs, non-medical costs, as well as income loss for TB patients and affected households in different settings, as well as the main drivers of those costs. Methods Eligibility criteria This review includes studies written in English, conducted in low- and middle-income countries and published from inception to March 31, 2013, reporting data on medical costs, non-medical costs and/or income loss incurred by TB patients during the process of seeking and receiving care for TB, as well as coping strategies. We excluded studies in which only total cost was reported without any disaggregation into direct and indirect costs and studies using secondary data derived from other published articles. Information sources and search strategies We searched the following electronic databases: PubMed; Global Information Full Text; Index Medicus for Africa, South-East Asia, Eastern Mediterranean region, and Western Pacific region; and Literatura Latinoamericana y del Caribe en Ciencias de la Salud. Furthermore, we checked reference lists of reviewed studies [19–22] and of documents and meeting reports from the World Bank and WHO websites. The search terms were “tuberculosis” (tuberculosis, TB, or tuberculosis as a MeSH Term in PubMed) and “cost” (cost(s), expense(s), economic, expenditure(s), payment(s), out-of-pocket, financial, impoverishment, or catastrophic). Evidence on residence and geographic context shows that urban–rural differences in tuberculosis costs are often mixed and not straightforwardly causal. The England and Wales study found that rural residence was associated with higher crude treatment non-completion, but after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, time since arrival in the UK, disease site, isoniazid resistance, and previous diagnosis, the association became non-significant [N1-F1]. This matters because it suggests that residence alone is not a stable determinant of cost in this design; instead, it is often confounded by sociodemographic and clinical factors. The same study also reports that urban areas had a much higher TB incidence rate than rural areas (6.3-fold higher) [N1-F1], which implies that urban–rural comparisons may reflect differences in disease burden and access to care, not just direct cost differences.

The evidence on cost components indicates that the most affected components by residence location are likely indirect costs and catastrophic cost outcomes, rather than a single direct medical component. A systematic review on financial burden reports that the mean total cost ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847, and that on average 20% of total cost was direct medical, 20% direct non-medical, and 60% income loss [N4-F4]. Another review similarly reports direct medical costs as the largest component, ranging from a mean of $0.03 to $17,140, while median costs ranged from $5.16 to higher values [N4-R3]. It also notes that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. This means that residence-related cost differences may be driven partly by pre-diagnosis costs, income loss, and coping mechanisms rather than only treatment-related direct costs.

On the question of whether urban vs rural differences persist across study designs, the evidence is limited and inconsistent. The England and Wales study adjusted for many confounders and found the association largely disappear, suggesting that study design matters: unadjusted urban–rural differences may be misleading [N1-F1]. The broader evidence base also includes a systematic review of urban–rural TB prevalence, but the provided excerpt does not give direct cost evidence [N1-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that urban vs rural differences in cost estimates are not robust across designs and are often explained by confounding variables [N1-F1], [N4-F4].

On reporting, the evidence shows that residence differences are reported in different forms. The England and Wales study is focused on treatment outcome and not on cost per se [N1-F1], but the broader financial-burden evidence reports total costs, mean total costs, and catastrophic cost as a percentage of income [N4-F4]. Another source notes that catastrophic cost is defined by total cost exceeding 20% of annual pre-TB household income [N1-R4]. So residence-related differences are reported as mean total costs, median costs, and catastrophic costs, but not uniformly across studies [N4-F4], [N1-R4]. The evidence is therefore thin on a single clean metric; residence differences are best interpreted as heterogeneous across cost measures.

In summary: urban vs rural differences are associated with higher crude treatment non-completion in one study, but not after adjustment [N1-F1]; the most affected cost components are indirect costs, income loss, and catastrophic burden [N4-F4]; study design and confounders greatly influence whether differences persist [N1-F1], [N4-F4]; and residence differences are reported as mean, median, and catastrophic cost, but not consistently in one measure [N4-F4], [N1-R4].

The evidence on hospitalization versus outpatient care shows that inpatient costs are generally much higher than outpatient costs, and this is especially true for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. A systematic synthesis of direct costs reports an average direct cost of treating and managing a TB case of $34,600 in 2015, and a multidrug-resistant TB case of $110,900 [N2-F2]. A separate study on TB care in individuals reports that DR-TB patients incurred the largest burden of costs, with a mean of $3,617 and median of $3,003 [N2-R2]. Another study on cost-effectiveness of multidrug-resistant TB treatment notes that outpatient care is more cost-effective than inpatient care, implying a strong cost differential [N2-R3]. A study on TB/HIV treatment also found higher costs of TB/HIV treatment when compared with TB treatment ($858 vs. $604) [N2-R5].

On the question of whether inpatient costs are mostly driven by length of stay or other services, the evidence is mixed. The Georgia study notes that inpatient financing was previously based on fixed tariffs per bed-day, which created perverse incentives for hospitalisation and prolonged stays [N3-F3]. It also reports that inpatient services were concentrated in urban areas and that a large proportion of DR-TB patients were hospitalised for 60 days in 2017–2018 [N3-F3]. However, the same study emphasizes that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, and that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs [N3-F3]. This suggests that inpatient cost differences are not only about length of stay but also about facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms. The California synthesis also breaks down direct costs into hospitalization, inpatient physician services, outpatient physician services, outpatient case management, laboratory and imaging tests, and anti-TB medications [N2-F2], showing that inpatient care is composed of multiple services, not just beds.

The evidence also indicates that treatment setting relates to follow-up and indirect costs. The financial-burden review reports that on average 60% of total cost was income loss, and that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It further notes that common coping mechanisms included taking loans and selling household items, and that costs as a percentage of income were particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. This means that outpatient care may be associated with more follow-up and indirect costs because patients are more likely to experience income loss and need ongoing social protection, whereas inpatient care may bundle some of those costs into the hospital stay. However, the evidence provided does not directly compare follow-up intensity by setting; the link is inferred from the composition of total costs [N4-F4].

Finally, cost definitions and denominators strongly affect comparisons between settings. The financial-burden review explicitly stratifies costs by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, and reports that cost as a percentage of income varies by setting [N4-F4]. The Georgia study compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and notes that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. The California synthesis also uses a perspective from the health care payer and adjusts costs to current values, emphasizing that estimates depend on the perspective and denominator used [N2-F2]. Therefore, comparisons between inpatient and outpatient settings are not reliable unless the cost definitions, denominators, and study perspective are aligned [N2-F2], [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

Overall, hospitalization increases mean costs substantially, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis [N2-F2], [N2-R3]; inpatient costs are influenced by length of stay, but also by facility type, tariffs, and financing [N3-F3]; treatment setting relates to follow-up and indirect costs through income loss and coping mechanisms [N4-F4]; and cost definitions and denominators are critical to valid comparisons between settings [N2-F2], [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

The evidence shows that study design and covariates are central to explaining cost variation. The financial-burden review reports that cost as a percentage of income was particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. The same source also stratifies data by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, indicating that socioeconomic status and disease severity are important covariates [N4-F4]. The Georgia study similarly compares unit costs across public and private facilities and notes that facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms affect cost estimates [N3-F3]. Together, these studies suggest that the most important covariates for explaining cost variation are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

Cost definitions and denominators affect mean cost estimates in several ways. The financial-burden review reports that mean total costs ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847, while direct medical costs accounted for about 20% of total cost on average [N4-F4]. It also notes that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment and that costs as a percentage of income vary by setting [N4-F4]. The Georgia study compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and finds that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. The California synthesis explicitly adjusts costs to current values using inflation-adjusted CPI components and reports direct cost components separately [N2-F2]. These examples show that mean cost estimates depend on whether costs are measured as total, direct medical, or income-loss-based, whether the denominator is per episode, per patient, or per household, and whether the study uses a health-system or household perspective [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

Study populations and follow-up periods affect post-diagnosis cost reporting. The financial-burden review includes data on costs incurred by patients and affected families during the process of seeking and receiving care, and it reports that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It also notes that cost as a percentage of income was especially high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB, implying that follow-up periods and disease progression matter [N4-F4]. The Georgia study uses a one-patient episode-of-care perspective and excludes surgical interventions, start-up costs, and costs of supporting change, which shapes what is counted as cost [N3-F3]. This matters because shorter follow-up periods may miss later indirect costs, while longer periods may capture income loss and coping mechanisms more fully [N4-F4]. The evidence does not give a single standard follow-up period, but it does show that post-diagnosis cost reporting is sensitive to the time window covered [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

Sample size and missing data affect precision and comparability. The financial-burden review explicitly mentions that studies were included if they reported medical costs, non-medical costs, or income loss, and that studies reporting only total cost without disaggregation were excluded [N4-F4]. It also reports that the systematic review included studies from low- and middle-income countries published up to March 2013, and that the search strategy included multiple databases and reference lists [N4-F4]. This suggests that the evidence base is heterogeneous and that missing data and publication bias may limit comparability. The Georgia study notes that sampling was pragmatic based on budget availability and that facilities were selected using different criteria, which can reduce precision if the sample is not representative [N3-F3]. The California synthesis likewise reports that most published cost estimates were based on data from the 1990s and that the study adjusted them to current values [N2-F2]. These details imply that small samples, incomplete data, and outdated data can reduce precision and make cross-study comparisons unreliable [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

In summary: the most important covariates are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode [N4-F4], [N3-F3]; cost definitions and denominators change mean cost estimates substantially [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2]; study populations and follow-up periods affect whether post-diagnosis cost reporting includes pre-diagnosis costs, income loss, and coping mechanisms [N4-F4], [N3-F3]; and sample size and missing data reduce precision and comparability, especially when data are outdated or collected from non-representative samples [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

Evidence on treatment location and facility type shows that public and private sector differences are real but often modest or context-dependent. The Georgia study reports that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, but there was very little difference between per-day costs for drug-susceptible treatment and NTP tariffs in inpatient services [N3-F3]. It also notes that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs [N3-F3]. Another source states that only three studies estimated the cost for TB patients treated in the private sector, covering a total of 102 patients, and that two of them were conducted in the same country [N3-R4]. This suggests that private-sector cost estimates are sparse and may not represent broad geographic or patient-level variation well [N3-R4]. The broader evidence base also indicates that private-sector engagement in TB care is an important policy issue, but the provided excerpts do not give a direct cost comparison across all high-burden countries [N3-R5].

The evidence suggests that facility type can explain differences in service and administrative costs. The Georgia study explicitly compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and finds that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. It also notes that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, implying that administrative and service costs differ by setting [N3-F3]. The California synthesis further breaks down direct costs into hospitalization, inpatient physician services, outpatient physician services, outpatient case management, laboratory and imaging tests, and anti-TB medications [N2-F2], showing that facility type can affect which services are included and how they are valued. However, the provided evidence does not directly attribute differences in administrative costs to one factor; the Georgia study implies that financing mechanisms and tariffs are part of the explanation [N3-F3].

Location interacts with treatment regimen or delivery mode in several ways. The Georgia study notes that the traditional financing approach of fixed tariffs per bed-day created a perverse incentive for hospitalisation for diagnosis and drug-susceptible TB treatment, and that 25% of drug-susceptible TB and 80% of drug-resistant TB patients were hospitalised for 30 and 60 days respectively [N3-F3]. ## Integrated synthesis of how patient residence, hospitalization, and treatment location affect mean post-diagnosis tuberculosis costs

The evidence across the four branches points to a consistent conclusion: tuberculosis cost estimates are shaped by multiple interacting factors, and residence, hospitalization, and treatment location each matter in different ways. The most important lesson is not that one factor alone explains costs, but that costs are context-dependent, heterogeneous, and highly sensitive to study design and measurement choices. The available evidence supports a layered explanation: residence and geography matter through access, service utilization, and socioeconomic context; hospitalization increases costs substantially, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; treatment location affects service composition, administrative costs, and unit prices; and study design, covariates, and definitions determine whether differences appear statistically meaningful or are simply artifacts of reporting.

---

## 1) Residence and geographic context: urban vs rural differences are mixed and often confounded

The evidence on residence shows that urban–rural differences in tuberculosis costs are not straightforwardly causal. In England and Wales, rural residence was associated with higher crude treatment non-completion, but after adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, time since arrival in the UK, disease site, isoniazid resistance, and previous diagnosis, the association became non-significant [N1-F1]. This suggests that residence alone is not a stable determinant of cost in this design; instead, it is often confounded by sociodemographic and clinical factors.

The broader cost evidence indicates that the most affected cost components by residence location are likely indirect costs and catastrophic burden rather than a single direct medical component. A financial-burden review reports that the mean total cost ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847, and that on average 20% of total cost was direct medical, 20% direct non-medical, and 60% income loss [N4-F4]. Another review similarly reports direct medical costs as the largest component, ranging from a mean of $0.03 to $17,140, while median costs ranged from $5.16 to higher values [N4-R3]. It also notes that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. This means that residence-related cost differences may be driven partly by pre-diagnosis costs, income loss, and coping mechanisms rather than only treatment-related direct costs.

On whether urban vs rural differences persist across study designs, the evidence is limited and inconsistent. The England and Wales study adjusted for many confounders and found the association largely disappear, suggesting that study design matters: unadjusted urban–rural differences may be misleading [N1-F1]. The broader evidence base also includes a systematic review of urban–rural TB prevalence, but the provided excerpt does not give direct cost evidence [N1-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that urban vs rural differences in cost estimates are not robust across designs and are often explained by confounding variables [N1-F1], [N4-F4].

On reporting, the evidence shows that residence differences are reported in different forms. The England and Wales study is focused on treatment outcome and not on cost per se [N1-F1], but the broader financial-burden evidence reports total costs, mean total costs, and catastrophic cost as a percentage of income [N4-F4]. Another source notes that catastrophic cost is defined by total cost exceeding 20% of annual pre-TB household income [N1-R4]. So residence-related differences are reported as mean total costs, median costs, and catastrophic costs, but not uniformly across studies [N4-F4], [N1-R4]. The evidence is therefore thin on a single clean metric; residence differences are best interpreted as heterogeneous across cost measures.

**Bottom line for residence:** residence and geographic context matter mainly through access, service utilization, and socioeconomic factors, but urban–rural differences are often confounded and not robust across study designs [N1-F1], [N4-F4]. The most affected cost components are indirect costs and catastrophic burden, not just direct medical costs [N4-F4].

---

## 2) Hospitalization versus outpatient care: inpatient costs are much higher, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis

The evidence on hospitalization versus outpatient care shows that inpatient costs are generally much higher than outpatient costs, and this is especially true for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. A systematic synthesis of direct costs reports an average direct cost of treating and managing a TB case of $34,600 in 2015, and a multidrug-resistant TB case of $110,900 [N2-F2]. A separate study on TB care in individuals reports that DR-TB patients incurred the largest burden of costs, with a mean of $3,617 and median of $3,003 [N2-R2]. Another study on cost-effectiveness of multidrug-resistant TB treatment notes that outpatient care is more cost-effective than inpatient care, implying a strong cost differential [N2-R3]. A study on TB/HIV treatment also found higher costs of TB/HIV treatment when compared with TB treatment ($858 vs. $604) [N2-R5].

On whether inpatient costs are mostly driven by length of stay or other services, the evidence is mixed. The Georgia study notes that inpatient financing was previously based on fixed tariffs per bed-day, which created perverse incentives for hospitalisation and prolonged stays [N3-F3]. It also reports that inpatient services were concentrated in urban areas and that a large proportion of DR-TB patients were hospitalised for 60 days in 2017–2018 [N3-F3]. However, the same study emphasizes that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, and that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs [N3-F3]. This suggests that inpatient cost differences are not only about length of stay but also about facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms. The California synthesis also breaks down direct costs into hospitalization, inpatient physician services, outpatient physician services, outpatient case management, laboratory and imaging tests, and anti-TB medications [N2-F2], showing that inpatient care is composed of multiple services, not just beds.

The evidence also indicates that treatment setting relates to follow-up and indirect costs. The financial-burden review reports that on average 60% of total cost was income loss, and that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It further notes that common coping mechanisms included taking loans and selling household items, and that costs as a percentage of income were particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. This means that outpatient care may be associated with more follow-up and indirect costs because patients are more likely to experience income loss and need ongoing social protection, whereas inpatient care may bundle some of those costs into the hospital stay. The financial-burden review explicitly stratifies costs by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, and reports that cost as a percentage of income varies by setting [N4-F4]. Therefore, comparisons between inpatient and outpatient settings are not reliable unless the cost definitions, denominators, and study perspective are aligned [N2-F2], [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

The Georgia study notes that the traditional financing approach of fixed tariffs per bed-day created a perverse incentive for hospitalisation for diagnosis and drug-susceptible TB treatment, and that 25% of drug-susceptible TB and 80% of drug-resistant TB patients were hospitalised for 30 and 60 days respectively [N3-F3]. ## 4) Study design and covariates: the most important factors are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode

The evidence shows that study design and covariates are central to explaining cost variation. The financial-burden review reports that cost as a percentage of income was particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. The same source also stratifies data by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, indicating that socioeconomic status and disease severity are important covariates [N4-F4]. The Georgia study similarly compares unit costs across public and private facilities and notes that facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms affect cost estimates [N3-F3]. Cost definitions and denominators affect mean cost estimates in several ways. The financial-burden review reports that mean total costs ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847, while direct medical costs accounted for about 20% of total cost on average [N4-F4]. The financial-burden review includes data on costs incurred by patients and affected families during the process of seeking and receiving care, and it reports that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It also notes that cost as a percentage of income was especially high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB, implying that follow-up periods and disease progression matter [N4-F4]. The evidence does not give a single standard follow-up period, but it does show that post-diagnosis cost reporting is sensitive to the time window covered [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

The financial-burden review explicitly mentions that studies were included if they reported medical costs, non-medical costs, or income loss, and that studies reporting only total cost without disaggregation were excluded [N4-F4]. It also reports that the systematic review included studies from low- and middle-income countries published up to March 2013, and that the search strategy included multiple databases and reference lists [N4-F4]. ## 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: patient residence, hospitalization, and treatment location each affect mean post-diagnosis tuberculosis costs, but in different ways and under different conditions. 

- **Residence and geography** matter mainly through access, socioeconomic context, and confounding variables, and urban–rural differences are often confounded and not robust across study designs [N1-F1], [N4-F4].
- **Hospitalization** substantially increases mean costs, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, but inpatient costs are influenced by length of stay, facility type, tariffs, and financing [N2-F2], [N3-F3].
- **Treatment location and facility type** show real but often modest differences, with private facilities generally more expensive than public providers in the Georgia evidence, while facility type can also explain service and administrative cost variation [N3-F3].
- **Study design and covariates** are central: socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode are the most important explanatory factors [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

In practical terms, the mean post-diagnosis cost of tuberculosis is not a single number; it depends on whether you measure total costs, direct costs, or catastrophic burden; whether you include pre-diagnosis costs and income loss; and how you define the study population, setting, and follow-up period [N4-F4], [N2-F2], [N3-F3]. A study on TB/HIV treatment also found higher costs of TB/HIV treatment when compared with TB treatment ($858 vs. $604) [N2-R5].

On whether inpatient costs are mostly driven by length of stay or other services, the evidence is mixed. The Georgia study notes that inpatient financing was previously based on fixed tariffs per bed-day, which created perverse incentives for hospitalisation and prolonged stays [N3-F3]. It also reports that inpatient services were concentrated in urban areas and that a large proportion of DR-TB patients were hospitalised for 60 days in 2017–2018 [N3-F3]. However, the same study emphasizes that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, and that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs [N3-F3]. This suggests that inpatient cost differences are not only about length of stay but also about facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms. The California synthesis also breaks down direct costs into hospitalization, inpatient physician services, outpatient physician services, outpatient case management, laboratory and imaging tests, and anti-TB medications [N2-F2], showing that inpatient care is composed of multiple services, not just beds.

The evidence also indicates that treatment setting relates to follow-up and indirect costs. The financial-burden review reports that on average 60% of total cost was income loss, and that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It further notes that common coping mechanisms included taking loans and selling household items, and that costs as a percentage of income were particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. This means that outpatient care may be associated with more follow-up and indirect costs because patients are more likely to experience income loss and need ongoing social protection, whereas inpatient care may bundle some of those costs into the hospital stay. However, the evidence provided does not directly compare follow-up intensity by setting; the link is inferred from the composition of total costs [N4-F4].

Finally, cost definitions and denominators strongly affect comparisons between settings. The financial-burden review explicitly stratifies costs by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, and reports that cost as a percentage of income varies by setting [N4-F4]. The Georgia study compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and finds that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. The California synthesis also uses a perspective from the health care payer and adjusts costs to current values, emphasizing that estimates depend on the perspective and denominator used [N2-F2]. Therefore, comparisons between inpatient and outpatient settings are not reliable unless the cost definitions, denominators, and study perspective are aligned [N2-F2], [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

**Bottom line for hospitalization:** hospitalization increases mean costs substantially, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis [N2-F2], [N2-R3]; inpatient costs are influenced by length of stay, but also by facility type, tariffs, and financing [N3-F3]; treatment setting relates to follow-up and indirect costs through income loss and coping mechanisms [N4-F4]; and cost definitions and denominators are critical to valid comparisons between settings [N2-F2], [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

## 3) Treatment location and facility type: public vs private differences are real but often modest or context-dependent

Evidence on treatment location and facility type shows that public and private sector differences are real but often modest or context-dependent. The Georgia study reports that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, but there was very little difference between per-day costs for drug-susceptible treatment and NTP tariffs in inpatient services [N3-F3]. It also notes that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs [N3-F3]. Another source states that only three studies estimated the cost for TB patients treated in the private sector, covering a total of 102 patients, and that two of them were conducted in the same country [N3-R4]. This suggests that private-sector cost estimates are sparse and may not represent broad geographic or patient-level variation well [N3-R4]. The broader evidence base also indicates that private-sector engagement in TB care is an important policy issue, but the provided excerpts do not give a direct cost comparison across all high-burden countries [N3-R5].

The evidence suggests that facility type can explain differences in service and administrative costs. The Georgia study explicitly compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and finds that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. It also notes that unit costs in private facilities were higher than in public providers, implying that administrative and service costs differ by setting [N3-F3]. The California synthesis further breaks down direct costs into hospitalization, inpatient physician services, outpatient physician services, outpatient case management, laboratory and imaging tests, and anti-TB medications [N2-F2], showing that facility type can affect which services are included and how they are valued. However, the provided evidence does not directly attribute differences in administrative costs to one factor; the Georgia study implies that financing mechanisms and tariffs are part of the explanation [N3-F3].

Location interacts with treatment regimen or delivery mode in several ways. The Georgia study notes that the traditional financing approach of fixed tariffs per bed-day created a perverse incentive for hospitalisation for diagnosis and drug-susceptible TB treatment, and that 25% of drug-susceptible TB and 80% of drug-resistant TB patients were hospitalised for 30 and 60 days respectively [N3-F3]. It also states that Georgia is moving toward a patient-centred approach by reducing hospitalisations and shifting to outpatient care [N3-F3]. The California synthesis similarly shows that outpatient case management includes clinic visits and case management personnel time, while inpatient services include hospitalization, inpatient physician services, and laboratory and imaging tests [N2-F2]. These examples show that delivery mode interacts with regimen complexity: drug-resistant TB is more expensive, hospitalisation is more common for resistant cases, and outpatient care requires different service components than inpatient care [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

The evidence is less clear on whether cost differences are explained by unit cost or patient-level factors. The Georgia study compares Value TB unit costs with NTP tariffs and reports that outpatient interventions costs exceeded tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. It also notes that treatment day financing exceeded actual costs in the capital for drug-resistant TB, and this was lower in the regions [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that both unit costs and patient-level factors matter: unit costs differ by facility and service, while patient-level factors such as disease severity, financing mechanisms, and location affect how much those unit costs are realized [N3-F3]. The financial-burden review also indicates that income loss and coping mechanisms vary by setting and that costs as a percentage of income were particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. This implies that patient-level factors such as poverty and disease severity can explain cost differences even when unit costs are comparable.

**Bottom line for treatment location:** public vs private facility location does affect cost estimates, with private facility unit costs generally higher than public provider costs in Georgia [N3-F3]; facility type can explain differences in service and administrative costs, as well as in how costs are valued against tariffs [N3-F3]; location interacts with treatment regimen or delivery mode, especially through hospitalisation and outpatient service composition [N3-F3], [N2-F2]; and cost differences are partly explained by unit cost, partly by patient-level factors such as disease severity and financing mechanisms [N3-F3], [N4-F4].

## 4) Study design and covariates: the most important factors are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode

The evidence shows that study design and covariates are central to explaining cost variation. The financial-burden review reports that cost as a percentage of income was particularly high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB [N4-F4]. The same source also stratifies data by socioeconomic status, hospitalisation, and other variables, indicating that socioeconomic status and disease severity are important covariates [N4-F4]. The Georgia study similarly compares unit costs across public and private facilities and notes that facility type, tariffs, and financing mechanisms affect cost estimates [N3-F3]. Together, these studies suggest that the most important covariates for explaining cost variation are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

Cost definitions and denominators affect mean cost estimates in several ways. The financial-burden review reports that mean total costs ranged from $55 to $8198, with an unweighted average of $847, while direct medical costs accounted for about 20% of total cost on average [N4-F4]. It also notes that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment and that costs as a percentage of income vary by setting [N4-F4]. The Georgia study compares top-down and bottom-up unit costs and finds that outpatient interventions costs exceeded NTP tariffs, while inpatient financing varied by region and facility type [N3-F3]. The California synthesis explicitly adjusts costs to current values using inflation-adjusted CPI components and reports direct cost components separately [N2-F2]. These examples show that mean cost estimates depend on whether costs are measured as total, direct medical, or income-loss-based, whether the denominator is per episode, per patient, or per household, and whether the study uses a health-system or household perspective [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

Study populations and follow-up periods affect post-diagnosis cost reporting. The financial-burden review includes data on costs incurred by patients and affected families during the process of seeking and receiving care, and it reports that half of total cost was incurred before TB treatment [N4-F4]. It also notes that cost as a percentage of income was especially high among poor people and those with multidrug-resistant TB, implying that follow-up periods and disease progression matter [N4-F4]. The Georgia study uses a one-patient episode-of-care perspective and excludes surgical interventions, start-up costs, and costs of supporting change, which shapes what is counted as cost [N3-F3]. This matters because shorter follow-up periods may miss later indirect costs, while longer periods may capture income loss and coping mechanisms more fully [N4-F4], [N3-F3]. The evidence does not give a single standard follow-up period, but it does show that post-diagnosis cost reporting is sensitive to the time window covered [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

Sample size and missing data affect precision and comparability. The financial-burden review explicitly mentions that studies were included if they reported medical costs, non-medical costs, or income loss, and that studies reporting only total cost without disaggregation were excluded [N4-F4]. It also reports that the systematic review included studies from low- and middle-income countries published up to March 2013, and that the search strategy included multiple databases and reference lists [N4-F4]. This suggests that the evidence base is heterogeneous and that missing data and publication bias may limit comparability. The Georgia study notes that sampling was pragmatic based on budget availability and that facilities were selected using different criteria, which can reduce precision if the sample is not representative [N3-F3]. The California synthesis likewise reports that most published cost estimates were based on data from the 1990s and that the study adjusted them to current values [N2-F2]. These details imply that small samples, incomplete data, and outdated data can reduce precision and make cross-study comparisons unreliable [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

**Bottom line for study design and covariates:** the most important covariates are socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode [N4-F4], [N3-F3]; cost definitions and denominators change mean cost estimates substantially [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2]; study populations and follow-up periods affect whether post-diagnosis cost reporting includes pre-diagnosis costs, income loss, and coping mechanisms [N4-F4], [N3-F3]; and sample size and missing data reduce precision and comparability, especially when data are outdated or collected from non-representative samples [N4-F4], [N3-F3], [N2-F2].

## 5) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: patient residence, hospitalization, and treatment location each affect mean post-diagnosis tuberculosis costs, but in different ways and under different conditions. 

- **Residence and geography** matter mainly through access, socioeconomic context, and confounding variables, and urban–rural differences are often confounded and not robust across study designs [N1-F1], [N4-F4].
- **Hospitalization** substantially increases mean costs, especially for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, but inpatient costs are influenced by length of stay, facility type, tariffs, and financing [N2-F2], [N3-F3].
- **Treatment location and facility type** show real but often modest differences, with private facilities generally more expensive than public providers in the Georgia evidence, while facility type can also explain service and administrative cost variation [N3-F3].
- **Study design and covariates** are central: socioeconomic status, disease severity, facility type, hospitalisation, and treatment regimen/delivery mode are the most important explanatory factors [N4-F4], [N3-F3].

In practical terms, the mean post-diagnosis cost of tuberculosis is not a single number; it depends on whether you measure total costs, direct costs, or catastrophic burden; whether you include pre-diagnosis costs and income loss; and how you define the study population, setting, and follow-up period [N4-F4], [N2-F2], [N3-F3]. For policy and program design, the evidence implies that cost reduction efforts should target both direct service delivery and the indirect burden of illness, while also improving measurement standards and reducing reliance on outdated or confounded estimates [N4-F4], [N2-F2], [N3-F3].
